title: Sell Mineral Rights in Garland, WY
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Garland, WY | Park County
metaDescription: Garland, WY takes its name from the Garland oil field in the Bighorn Basin. Get a real cash offer for your Park County mineral or royalty interest.
heroLead: Garland is a Bighorn Basin oil town in the plainest sense, the community took its name from the field that put it on the map.
intro: Garland Field has been producing since the early 1900s, one of the structural anticline discoveries that made this part of Park County an early Wyoming oil center. Ownership here has passed through generations of the same ranching families that homesteaded the ground before oil was ever found on it.

sections.heading: A century of Garland field production
paragraphs: Like Elk Basin and Oregon Basin nearby, Garland's shallow structural traps have been re-drilled and re-worked repeatedly since discovery. Current activity is mostly low-volume stripper production under independent operators, with occasional secondary recovery projects extending well life beyond what the original drillers expected.

sections.heading: Old leases, older mineral deeds
paragraphs: Because Garland's history runs back over a century, mineral owners here sometimes hold deeds with unclear or outdated language, referencing entities and terms that predate modern lease forms. That's not a problem for selling, but it does mean a title check matters more than it would on newer Powder River Basin acreage.

sections.heading: What determines your offer
paragraphs: Current production volume on your specific tract, decline rate, and whether the well count on your acreage has grown or shrunk in recent years. Bring recent check stubs and your division order if you have one; without them, expect the offer process to start with a title and production pull instead.

sections.heading: Secondary recovery and what it means for owners
paragraphs: Some Garland field wells have gone through waterflood or other secondary recovery projects over the decades, which can extend a well's producing life well past its original decline curve. If your check has held steadier than expected for an old field, a secondary recovery project on your unit may be the reason.

faqs.question: Is Garland field still active?
faqs.answer: Yes, mostly stripper-level production from wells drilled decades ago, operated by independents working legacy Bighorn Basin leases.

faqs.question: My deed language looks old-fashioned, is that a problem?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily, but it means a careful title review before closing any sale. Park County Clerk records in Cody can help fill in gaps.

faqs.question: How much does field age affect value?
faqs.answer: Less than current production and decline trend do. An old field with steady low-volume output can still price reasonably against those metrics.

faqs.question: How do I find out if my well is on secondary recovery?
faqs.answer: Your division order or operator statement sometimes notes it. Otherwise, the Park County Clerk or Wyoming Oil and Gas Conservation Commission can confirm the well's current production method.
